JERUSALEM — Israeli troops raided Gaza’s largest hospital, al-Shifa, in what the Israel Defense Forces called a “precise and targeted operation against Hamas” early Wednesday. Israel and the United States have asserted that Hamas is using hospitals — including Shifa — and the tunnels underneath them for its military operations. Hamas has denied that. Details of the raid, which the IDF said began around 2 a.m. local time, remain murky because of ongoing communications outages, Israeli bombardments and ground fighting.

Videos and photos released by the IDF later in the day showed an alleged haul of 11 guns, three military vests — one with a Hamas logo — and nine grenades that the IDF said were pulled from the hospital’s radiology unit. The Washington Post was unable to independently verify who the weapons belonged to or how they came to be inside the radiology unit.

At a news conference late Wednesday, President Biden said he has been “deeply involved” in the negotiations to release the roughly 240 foreign and Israeli hostages held by Hamas in Gaza. “I have gotten great cooperation from the Qataris,” Biden said, adding that he was “mildly hopeful” a deal would get done.
Here’s what to know

content: Hamas has agreed in principle and Israel is now considering a proposal for the release of at least 50 women and children among about 240 foreign and Israeli hostages being held by Hamas in Gaza, an Arab diplomat familiar with the negotiations told The Post. In exchange, Israel would agree to a three-to-five-day pause “in place” in the fighting, increased humanitarian aid to Gaza, and the release of an unspecified number of women and children held in Israeli prisons.

Some 700 patients were present at al-Shifa Hospital during the raid, along with more than 400 health workers and about 3,000 displaced people who had sought refuge there, according to the latest U.N. figures.

A fuel tanker entered Gaza via the Rafah border crossing Wednesday for the first time since the war began. A Gaza-based U.N. official said Israel has restricted the use of the fuel to transporting aid from the Egyptian border, so it could not be used for Gaza’s water systems or hospitals. The fuel shipment was “only 9 percent of what we need daily to sustain lifesaving activities,” said the official, Thomas White.

National Security Council spokesman John Kirby said Tuesday that the United States has information that Hamas has used hospitals in the Gaza Strip, including Shifa, and tunnels underneath them for its military operations and to hold hostages, although he added that “hospitals and patients must be protected.” The Post could not independently verify the situation on the ground or Kirby’s claim.

The Gaza Health Ministry said Friday that about 11,100 Palestinians had been killed in Gaza since Oct. 7. The ministry says that the toll is now far higher but that it is no longer able to provide official numbers, citing communications blackouts and fighting around hospitals.

items.content: Today’s key developments in the Israel-Gaza war
By Sammy Westfall

authors.name: Sammy Westfall
authors.bio: Sammy Westfall is an assistant editor on The Washington Post's Foreign desk.
authors.expertise: Assistant Editor on the Foreign desk

items.content: Here are the biggest news items from the Israel-Gaza war on Nov. 15.

By Wednesday night local time, Israeli forces were still inside al-Shifa Hospital, Gaza’s largest, in pursuit of Hamas fighters they allege operate from tunnels under the facility, Israeli military and Gaza health officials said. Munir al-Bursh, director general of the Gaza Health Ministry, told The Washington Post by phone around 7 p.m. that Israeli “tanks retreated to around the hospital but that soldiers remained.” The hospital is a refuge for thousands of terrified patients, overworked doctors and displaced civilians.

The Israeli military released two videos and some photos from its raid on al-Shifa Hospital showing what it said were Hamas weapons and other gear recovered from the complex. The Post was unable to independently verify to whom the weapons belonged or how they came to be inside the hospital’s radiology unit.

The late-night operation at Shifa was the culmination of weeks of messaging from Israeli officials about alleged Hamas infiltration of hospitals in Gaza, The Post’s Louisa Loveluck and Meg Kelly report. Israeli officials have been asserting for weeks, while offering little public evidence, that the Hamas militant group has a command center below the hospital, making it a legitimate military target. U.S. officials have backed the claim.

Hamas has agreed in principle and Israel is now considering a proposal for the release of at least 50 women and children among about 240 foreign and Israeli hostages being held by Hamas, according to an Arab diplomat familiar with the negotiations. In exchange for the hostages, Israel would agree to a three- to five-day pause “in place” in the fighting, increased humanitarian aid to Gaza, and the release of an unspecified number of women and children held in Israeli prisons.

At a news conference following his meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, President Biden said he doesn’t think the conflict in Gaza will end until there is a two-state solution. Biden also said he has been “deeply involved” in the hostage release negotiations, and that he was “mildly hopeful” a deal would get done. “I don’t want to get ahead of myself here because I don’t know what’s happened in the last four hours, but I have gotten great cooperation from the Qataris,” Biden said.

The U.N. Security Council passed its first unified statement on the conflict nearly six weeks after it began. The resolution demanded “immediate extended humanitarian pauses” in the fighting in Gaza, the unhindered supply of humanitarian assistance to civilians there and the unconditional release of all hostages.

items.content: SAN FRANCISCO — President Biden on Wednesday blamed Hamas for committing the “first war crime” in the bloody standoff over Gaza’s al-Shifa Hospital by having its military headquarters “hidden under” the large hospital complex.

The Israel Defense Forces released images and video from the hospital Wednesday showing small arms and military uniforms around hospital equipment such as MRI machines. Israeli officials pointed to radio equipment and discs as evidence of a Hamas command center.

The footage did not include proof of an underground tunnel network or substantiate Israel’s allegations that an underground Hamas complex sat beneath Shifa. Israeli officials said they were still in the process of infiltrating the facility, Gaza’s largest hospital.
How Israel built its case to raid Gaza’s al-Shifa Hospital

Israel has faced widespread criticism for the enormous civilian death toll of its offensive against Hamas. Israeli officials blame Hamas for embedding inside civilian infrastructure in Gaza, one of the most densely populated places on earth.

White House spokesman John Kirby, when asked whether the images fell short of corroborating Israeli claims of a major Hamas command center, said the United States remains “comfortable” with a declassified intelligence assessment that Hamas has used and is using Shifa as a “command and control node.”

Hamas denies using the hospital for military purposes, which would amount to a war crime. The militant group has invited international groups to visit and observe Gaza hospitals but the fighting has not allowed for it.

Speaking at a news conference following a meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Biden also told reporters that he has been “deeply involved” in the negotiations to release the roughly 240 foreign and Israeli hostages being held by Hamas in Gaza.

“I don’t want to get ahead of myself here because I don’t know what’s happened in the last four hours, but I have gotten great cooperation from the Qataris,” Biden said, adding that he was “mildly hopeful” a deal would get done.

Biden also said that he thought the war would end when Hamas no longer has the ability to do “horrific things” to Israelis, adding that he warned Israel that trying to occupy the Gaza Strip would be a “big mistake.”
“I think the only ultimate answer here is a two-state solution,” Biden said.

Visual evidence appears to show graves at al-Shifa Hospital
By Jarrett Ley and Meg Kelly

authors.name: Meg Kelly
authors.bio: Meg Kelly is a video reporter for The Washington Post's Visual Forensics team.
authors.expertise: Video reporter, Visual Forensics

items.fullcaption: Satellite imagery appears to show that tents were moved to reveal a thin patch of earth at al-Shifa Hospital complex on Nov. 14. (Maxar/Planet)
items.blurb: Satellite imagery appears to show that tents were moved to reveal a thin patch of earth at al-Shifa Hospital complex on Nov. 14.

items.content: An image posted to X on Tuesday and geolocated by The Washington Post shows several people, including one in medical scrubs, digging at least two trenches into the soil at al-Shifa Hospital, providing powerful visual evidence to back up reports of ad hoc graves being established for dying patients.

The most visible of the two trenches, which was still in progress at the time the photograph was taken, is rectilinear and measures about three feet deep and six feet at its widest, according to The Post’s analysis.

Satellite imagery taken Tuesday and provided to The Post by Planet Labs appears to show that tents were moved and reveals a thin patch of earth in the same place as the photograph, according to a comparison of satellite imagery. The location had been covered as recently as Sunday, comparison of satellite imagery showed.

Gaza Health Ministry director Medhat Abbas warned that bodies have been piling up for days. He estimated on Tuesday that at least 100 bodies were decomposing around the hospital, including 50 inside. As Israeli forces drew closer to the hospital, it was too dangerous to evacuate the dead, leaving hospital staff with little choice but to prepare a mass grave for 180, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs wrote in a news release.

The grave probably was dug sometime Tuesday, when the image of it first surfaced. Just before Israeli forces entered the hospital complex early Wednesday, Munir al-Bursh, director general of the Gaza Health Ministry, described the grave in an audio recording posted to social media in which he appears to be speaking with an Israeli officer.
“When you come in you’re going to see 100 bodies on one side, and a mass grave full of 80 people on another,” he said. “These are patients that have all died.”
The Post could not independently verify the recording, and the identity of the Israeli officer al-Bursh spoke to was not immediately clear.

items.content: The Israeli military released two videos and some photos Wednesday from the al-Shifa Hospital showing what it said were Hamas weapons and other gear recovered from the complex.

The majority of both videos appears to have been filmed inside the hospital’s radiology unit, called the Prince Nayef Center, located next to the emergency room in the heart of the al-Shifa complex. In the longer video, Israel Defense Forces (IDF) spokesman Jonathan Conricus gives a single-shot tour of the building, pausing periodically to show where he said Hamas had hidden “go bags.”

He ducks behind an MRI machine to show viewers a backpack with an AK-style rifle and ammunition visible. He then moves down the hall, pausing at a closet where he said four AK-style self-loading rifles with folding stocks were found.

Photographs released later by the IDF appeared to show the full alleged haul, laid out neatly: military uniforms, 11 guns, three military vests, one with a Hamas logo, nine grenades, two Qurans, a string of prayer beads, a box of dates.
The Washington Post was unable to independently verify who the weapons belonged to or how they came to be inside the radiology unit.

“These arms by themselves hardly seem to justify the military fixation on al-Shifa, even setting the law aside,” said Brian Finucane, a senior adviser at the International Crisis Group and former legal adviser at the State Department.

Pressed in an interview Wednesday on CNN, another IDF spokesman, Richard Hecht, was cautious in his comments about what the raid had revealed. “We found certain things,” he said. “That’s all I can say at this stage.”
IDF forces found no sign of hostages at the site, Israel’s Army Radio reported.

items.content: In 2014, both Israel and Ukraine featured in conflicts that would set the stage for what we see today. But there was no comparison when it came to whom Americans sympathized with more. While a Gallup poll showed 17 percent considered Ukraine an ally, nearly half — 44 percent — said the same of Israel.
This was, of course, broadly reflective of the United States’ long-standing foreign policy toward Israel, as well as its more complicated and less consequential relationship with Ukraine.

items.content: The U.N. Security Council passed a resolution on Wednesday demanding “immediate extended humanitarian pauses” in the fighting in Gaza, the unhindered supply of humanitarian assistance to civilians there and the unconditional release of all hostages, in its first unified statement on the conflict.

Russia and the United States, along with Britain, abstained from the vote, objecting to the fact that the resolution did not contain key items they sought, but acknowledging international dismay over Security Council paralysis in the face of the ongoing loss of life.

Four previous resolutions had failed, with U.S. vetoes over the absence of a condemnation of Hamas and Israel’s right to respond, and Russia vetoing a U.S.-drafted resolution that did not call for a full cease-fire. Neither measure was in Wednesday’s resolution, which was drafted and introduced by Malta and approved by it and the other 11 members.

Israeli forces remain inside al-Shifa hospital
By Miriam Berger and Hazem Balousha

authors.name: Miriam Berger

items.content: JERUSALEM — Israeli forces are still inside al-Shifa Hospital, the Israeli military said in a statement. Munir al-Bursh, the director general of hospitals in Gaza, confirmed the news to The Washington Post by phone from inside the besieged compound.

“The IDF is continuing to operate in the hospital complex,” the military said in a statement issued around 8:20 p.m. local time, about 18 hours after Israeli forces said they would raid Gaza’s largest hospital.

Bursh told The Post by phone around 7 p.m. that Israeli “tanks retreated to around the hospital but that soldiers remained in the hospital” and were stationed in four buildings. In a second call, about an hour later, he confirmed that Israeli forces still were present.
The details of Israel’s raid and conditions inside the hospital remain unclear because communication outages, ground fighting and Israeli bombardments make access difficult.
Balousha reported from Amman, Jordan.

items.content: A U.S. Navy destroyer shot down a drone in the Red Sea that came from Yemen, U.S. defense officials said Wednesday, marking at least the second known time since the Israel-Gaza war began last month that American warships have brought down aerial threats.

“The USS Thomas Hudner engaged a drone that originated from Yemen, and was heading in the direction of the ship. The drone was destroyed and there were no U.S. casualties,” said Lt. Cmdr. Emily Pumphrey, a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command.

The destroyer was transiting international waters in the Red Sea when the incident occurred, a U.S. defense official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of ongoing operations.

It was not immediately clear who launched the drone or whether the ship was the target, but U.S. officials have blamed Houthi rebels, an Iranian-backed militant group that controls large swaths of Yemen, for two other recent incidents in the Red Sea.

The Houthis shot down a $30 million U.S. Reaper drone off the coast of Yemen on Nov. 8, the Pentagon has said. Last month, another U.S. ship, the USS Carney, shot down missiles fired toward Israel from Yemen.

items.content: Martin Griffiths, head of the United Nations humanitarian agency, OCHA, released a 10-point plan to “rein in the carnage” in the Gaza Strip, which he said is reaching “new levels of horror every day.”

Among the points in the plan was a call to open additional border crossings for aid to enter Gaza. Specifically, he said, the crossing at Kerem Shalom, a kibbutz in southern Israel near the Egyptian and Gazan borders, should be opened. During the conflict, only the Rafah crossing between Egypt and Gaza has been opened periodically.

He also said the United Nations and other organizations should be allowed to access fuel to deliver aid and “provide basic services.” U.N. humanitarian workers received fuel Wednesday, but were only allowed to use it to transport aid from the Rafah crossing, and not for other purposes the United Nations says are necessary, such as powering generators at medical facilities. Israel has restricted the use of fuel being brought into Gaza, citing concerns that Hamas could divert it for military use.

The plan also calls for the implementation of a “humanitarian ceasefire,” which Griffiths said would allow basic services to resume. “Such a ceasefire is also vital to facilitate the delivery of aid, allow the release of hostages, and provide respite to civilians,” he said.

items.content: “I don’t think it’s very safe to evacuate [al-Shifa] Hospital right now,” said Alyona Synenko, a spokeswoman for the International Committee of the Red Cross.
She said people at the hospital “say if they open the door, they risk being shot, as the fighting has been relentless.”
Synenko called for people to be able to evacuate safely, but added, “even those who do not evacuate are still protected by international humanitarian law. They are still civilians.”

items.content: JERUSALEM — Salma Tarabin is eight months pregnant, praying the war ends before her third child is born into a “poisoned” world. The 30-year-old is exhausted, hungry and sick from drinking dirty water. For a month now, she has been sleeping on a sheet on a hard classroom floor with more than 80 other women and children, she told The Washington Post by phone. The men and older boys sleep outside in the courtyard of what was formerly a school run by UNRWA, the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees, in the southern Gazan city of Rafah.
This is an excerpt from a full story.

items.content: John Kirby, the National Security Council spokesman, said at a briefing Wednesday that the United States “did not give an okay” to Israel’s raid of al-Shifa Hospital, as it does not give prior approval to Israel’s tactical operations. “The United States is not involved in those procedures,” he said.
Kirby reaffirmed the White House’s recent position on the place of hospitals in the conflict.
“We don’t want to see innocent civilians, patients, medical staff become victims of crossfire,” Kirby said. “We believe hospitals should be protected.”

Israel’s raid on the hospital has drawn international scrutiny amid an already staggering Palestinian civilian death toll. Israel says it is conducting a narrow operation at the hospital to root out Hamas militants it says are operating there. Hamas denies the assertion.

Correction: A previous version of this post mischaracterized remarks made by John Kirby, the National Security Council spokesman. He said that the U.S. does not give prior approval to Israel’s tactical operations, not that the U.S. did not approve of Israel’s operation in Shifa. The post has been corrected.

items.content: A growing number of Americans say Israel has gone too far in its response to the Oct. 7 attack by Hamas, according to a poll this month by Marist, NPR and PBS NewsHour.

According to the poll, conducted Nov. 6-9, 38 percent of Americans say that Israel’s response to the attack — which killed about 1,200 Israelis — has been “too much.” That is up from 26 percent who gave the same response last month.
Another 38 percent of Americans said this month that Israel’s response has been “about right.” Last month, 44 percent said Israel’s response was “about right.”
The number of Americans who think Israel’s response is insufficient has shrunk, from 27 percent last month to 17 percent this month.
The figures suggest growing discontent among Americans with Israel’s response.

The skyrocketing number of civilian deaths in Israel’s war in Gaza has sparked growing international outcry. The Gaza Health Ministry has been unable to provide an official death toll in recent days because of the combat situation, but it said that as of Friday, about 11,100 Palestinians had been killed since the start of the war.

The NPR/PBS/Marist survey this month of 1,429 adults had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points; last month’s survey of 1,313 adults had a sampling error margin of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points.
